text: COUNTY COUNCIL OF ANNE ARUNDEL COUNTY, MARYLAND AGENDA Legislative Session 2026, Legislative Day No. 17 Monday, September 21, 2026 – 6:00 P.M. County Council Chambers 44 Calvert Street Annapolis, Maryland A. Call to Order B. Invocation (Fiedler) C. Pledge of Allegiance D. Ethics Statement E. Invitation to Audience F. Announcement of Items Not Appearing on Agenda G. Preliminary Motion H. Approval of Minutes September 8, 2026 – Legislative Day No. 16 I. Introduction of Bills BILL NO. 75-26 – AN ORDINANCE concerning: Current Expense Budget – Supplementary Appropriations – Chief Administrative Office – Technical Corrections of Annual Budget and Appropriation Ordinance – FOR the purpose of making supplementary appropriations from contingent funds in the general fund of the County for the current fiscal year; making certain technical corrections to the Annual Budget and Appropriation Ordinance to align with changes made through amendments to the Ordinance; and generally relating to making supplementary appropriations to the Current Expense Budget and the Annual Budget and Appropriation Ordinance for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2027. Introduced by Ms. Hummer, Chair (by request of the County Executive) BILL NO. 76-26 – AN ORDINANCE concerning: Subdivision and Development – Development Requirements – Cottage Homes – County Residency Requirement – FOR the purpose of requiring the initial sale of a cottage home to be to a county resident; requiring the transfer within twenty years of purchase be made to a county resident; and generally relating to subdivision and development. Introduced by Ms. Rodvien Agenda September 21, 2026 Page 2 J. Introduction of Resolutions RESOLUTION NO. 32-26 – RESOLUTION confirming the appointment of a County resident and a member of the classified service to serve on the Pension Oversight Commission for Anne Arundel County Introduced by Ms. Hummer, Chair (by request of the County Executive) RESOLUTION NO. 33-26 – RESOLUTION approving submission of names for the Property Tax Assessment Appeal Board Introduced by Ms. Hummer, Chair (by request of the County Executive) K. Public Hearings and Call of Bills and Resolutions for Final Reading and/or Vote BILL NO. 59-26 (Hearing Concluded/Eligible for Vote) (Amendment Proposed) – AN ORDINANCE concerning: Public Ethics – Conflicts of Interest – County Council – FOR the purpose of amending the definition of “legislative action”; defining “participation”; expanding the types of presumed conflicts of interest that would prohibit a Councilmember from participating in legislative action to include Councilmembers and their immediate family members; and generally relating to public ethics. Introduced by Mr. Volke BILL NO. 60-26 (Hearing Concluded/Eligible for Vote) – AN ORDINANCE concerning: Finance, Taxation, and Budget – Community Benefit Program – Grants for Councilmanic Districts – FOR the purpose of adding all Councilmanic districts as eligible for grants under the Community Benefit Program under certain circumstances; establishing certain grants to be applied for and approved by individual Councilmembers and funded by the County Executive’s budget under certain circumstances; and generally relating to finance, taxation, and budget. Introduced by Mr. Volke BILL NO. 61-26 (As Amended) (Amendment(s) Proposed) – AN ORDINANCE concerning: Public Safety – Zoning – Article 18 Update – FOR the purpose of adding and modifying definitions of certain terms; removing the definitions of certain obsolete terms; revising certain general provisions; providing for the scope, administration, and interpretation of the Zoning Code; adding legacy provisions applicable to certain development applications and zoning certificates of use; establishing certain requirements for zoning certificate of use applications; establishing exemptions to bulk regulations for dwellings in existence as of a certain date; modifying certain parking space requirements; adding purpose clauses for certain zoning districts; modifying, adding, and removing certain uses allowed in certain zoning districts under certain circumstances; clarifying certain bulk regulations in certain districts; removing the Open Space Conservation Overlay as obsolete; modifying certain requirements for certain conditional uses; modifying certain requirements for certain special exception uses; modifying certain provisions pertaining to certain special uses; modifying certain provisions pertaining to nonconforming uses; establishing standards for decisions on nonconforming use applications and prohibiting subsequent nonconforming use applications; modifying Agenda September 21, 2026 Page 3 certain provisions pertaining to applications and hearings before the Administrative Hearing Officer; clarifying the requirements for keeping a variance or special exception from expiring; modifying certain provisions pertaining to certain enforcement and penalties; clarifying certain existing provisions; making certain technical and stylistic changes; correcting references to State Code provisions; correcting certain crossreferences; and generally relating to public safety, and zoning. Introduced by Ms. Hummer, Chair (by request of the County Executive) BILL NO. 62-26 – AN EMERGENCY ORDINANCE concerning: Zoning – Conditional Use Requirements – Licensed Dispensaries of Cannabis – FOR the purpose of requiring a licensed dispensary be located a certain distance from certain facilities; making this Ordinance an emergency measure; and generally relating to zoning. Introduced by Mr. Volke BILL NO. 63-26 (Amendment Proposed) – AN ORDINANCE concerning: Zoning – Data Storage Center – FOR the purpose of modifying the definition of “data storage center”; grandfathering certain data storage centers; removing certain parking requirements for data storage centers; removing certain data storage centers as an allowable use in certain commercial, industrial, mixed use, and Odenton Town Center districts; removing the conditional use requirements for certain data storage centers; making certain technical and stylistic changes; and generally related to zoning. Introduced by Mr. Volke BILL NO. 64-26 – AN ORDINANCE concerning: Zoning – Conditional Uses – Workforce Housing – FOR the purpose of reducing the density of housing in R5 for workforce housing under certain circumstances; and generally relating to zoning. Introduced by Mr. Volke BILL NO. 65-26 (Amendment(s) Proposed) – AN ORDINANCE concerning: Public Ethics – Campaign Contribution Disclosure and Comprehensive Zoning Integrity Act – FOR the purpose of adding a definition for “applicant”, “covered person”, and “zoning text amendment”; requiring certain campaign contribution disclosures from applicants for certain land use determinations, zoning text amendment legislation, and land use legislative actions; prohibiting certain campaign contributions during certain zoning processes; providing for a delayed effective date; and generally related to public ethics. Introduced by Mr. Volke BILL NO. 66-26 (Amendment Proposed) – AN ORDINANCE concerning: Public Ethics – Enforcement – County Council – FOR the purpose of authorizing the Ethics Commission to impose a civil penalty for a violation of the public ethics law; authorizing the Ethics Commission to dispose of a complaint by consent order; establishing procedures for the assessment, collection, waiver, and reduction of a civil penalty imposed by the Ethics Commission; allowing for judicial review of a final order of the Ethics Commission for certain unpaid civil penalties; and generally relating to public ethics. Introduced by Mr. Volke BILL NO. 67-26 (Amendment Proposed) – AN ORDINANCE concerning: Zoning – BWI Mixed Use Overlay Area – FOR the purpose of amending the BWI Mixed Use Overlay Area Map; and generally relating to zoning. Background: CivicPlus has been the City’s website provider for more than 8 years. In addition to the website, the City uses three CivicPlus programs that support communications, accessibility, emergency notification, and records management that are covered under this contract. Staff is seeking Council approval to renew these services. Two years ago, the City added increased website accessibility to support compliance with ADA requirements and accessibility standards through their AudioEye platform. The AudioEye tool is featured at the bottom of every page. The accessibility features help people with visual impairments or other needs better use and access our website. Some features include contrast changes, adjusting text size, adjusting fonts, removing animations, color shifts, highlighting and cursor adjustments. The City also uses CivicPlus’s Emergency Notification system to enhance our communications outreach to our residents, for major announcements and during emergency situations. The system allows City staff to mass notify/text subscribers and can also issue targeted alerts to those within certain geographic areas for emergencies, severe weather, or public safety incidents. You don’t need to be a subscriber to get a geographic emergency alert, however staff recommend that residents still subscribe so that we have the most accurate contact information. Internally, HR also uses the software to reach employees for a variety of needs and notices. Currently, there are more than 700 subscribers from the public. Finally, the City uses social media archiving to preserve content from its social media accounts, including posts and comments. This is done in support of the City’s record retention policy and to ensure compliance with any public records requests that the City may receive. With more than five social media profiles, reaching thousands of residents and people daily, the service provides a centralized and user-friendly way for staff to maintain these records. City Engineer Proposed Consent: Yes Originating Department: Department of Public Works Action Requested: Removal of 6 Pay-to-Park Spaces on East Side of Yale Avenue between Lehigh Road and College Avenue Strategic Plan Objective: Enhance safety and quality of enforcement to advance our reputation as a safe City. Background/Justification: City staff have been asked to identify the impacts of removing the 6 currently metered pay-to-park spaces on the east side of Yale Avenue between Lehigh Road and College Avenue. The 7400-Block of Yale Avenue is one block east of Baltimore Avenue and runs to the rear of City Hall to connect Knox Road with College Avenue. Previously, the entire 7400-Block of Yale Avenue had metered pay-to-park spaces on the east side of the roadway. However, to accommodate the angled parking behind City Hall, the spaces on the east side of the roadway were removed between Knox Road and Lehigh Road during the construction of City Hall. Between Lehigh Road and College Avenue, Yale Avenue is 26-feet wide with a 9’ southbound lane, 9’ northbound lane, and 8’ parking lane adjacent to northbound traffic. There are currently 3 smart meters that service the 6 pay-to-park spaces that are currently proposed to transition to mobile app payment spaces as effective October 1, 2026. The 2025 revenue for these spaces was $9,159.85, and the 2026 YTD revenue as of September 10 is $7,137.71. However, City staff are now recommending consideration of removal of these parking spaces to align Yale Avenue between Lehigh Road and College Avenue with the segment immediately to the south, improve traffic flow at the intersection of Yale Avenue and College Avenue, and enhance pedestrian safety and accessibility. From 2019 to present, there were two crashes within the study area per Maryland State Police Crash Data. On 10/6/2021, there was a head-on property damage collision on Yale Avenue just south of the intersection with College Avenue involving 2 vehicles at 4:43pm. On 5/19/2024, there was a same-direction sideswipe property damage crash involving 2 vehicles on northbound Yale Avenue between Lehigh Road and College Avenue at 9:30am. Due to the narrow turn radius at the intersection of College Avenue and Yale Avenue for eastbound vehicles turning onto Yale Avenue, drivers of certain larger vehicles must wait for northbound Yale Avenue traffic to clear the intersection to make a right turn or drive onto the sidewalk to avoid hitting northbound traffic which 009 presents a hazard to the high volume of pedestrian traffic at the intersection. The removal of the parking would allow the centerline of the roadway to be adjusted approximately 4’ to improve the turn radius for traffic. Staff observed numerous service vehicles navigating the intersection to provide deliveries, refuse collection, and other services at nearby residential and commercial properties. Additionally, removal of the meters and meter poles on the sidewalk would improve pedestrian accessibility to allow for a continuous 4-foot wide sidewalk between Knox Road and College Avenue. Adjacent streets including the 4500-Blocks of College Avenue and Lehigh Road and the City’s Parking Garage one block to the south can accommodate additional parking volume that may be displaced from these 6 spaces. Equity and Inclusion Impact: Installation of a prohibited parking zone is anticipated to improve safety and accessibility for all users of the roadway. Fiscal Impact: Reduction of approximately $9,000-$10,000 in Annual Parking Meter, Mobile App and Citation Revenue. Council Options: 1. Direct the Department of Public Works and Department of Public Services staff to remove 6 Pay-to-Park Spaces on the east side of Yale Avenue between Lehigh Road and College Avenue. 2. Request additional information. 3. Leave the roadway in the current configuration. Staff Recommendation: Option 1 - Direct the Department of Public Works and Department of Public Services staff to remove 6 Payto-Park Spaces on the east side of Yale Avenue between Lehigh Road and College Avenue. Recommended Motion: I move to direct the Department of Public Works and Department of Public Services to remove 6 pay-to-park spaces on the east side of Yale Avenue between Lehigh Road and College Avenue. Once adopted, these priorities serve as the basis for the City’s advocacy positions throughout the legislative session. The Rules of Procedure establish roles for staff and the City’s contracted lobbyists in monitoring legislation, identifying emerging issues and opportunities, and conducting advocacy that is consistent with the Council’s adopted priorities. Council may revise or supplement its priorities during the legislative session as needed. The Rules also allow staff and the legislative team to respond quickly as legislation develops. Written correspondence, testimony, and statements of position that clearly align with the Council’s adopted priorities may be issued without returning to Council for approval each time. Council will be notified when the City submits a position of support or opposition. Development of the 2027 priorities began earlier this year with the City’s participation in the Maryland Municipal League (MML) Legislative Action Request (LAR) process. In May, the Council authorized the submission of three (3) proposals for MML consideration: prohibiting stopping or standing in bike lanes; outof-cycle commercial property assessments; and a statewide study/task force on vacant commercial properties. In June, the Mayor and Council were invited to submit potential priority policy areas and potential legislative proposals for the 2027 session through a survey and to participate in individual discussions with staff and the City’s legislative representatives. Seventeen proposals were submitted through the survey. Staff and the City’s legislative team presented the results at the July 14 Council meeting. During July and August, staff and the legislative team met individually with the Mayor and Councilmembers to further discuss their proposals, refine ideas, and identify potential legislative and advocacy strategies. Best, 26-G-92 CivicPlus Renewal From: Chad Hora Sent: Monday, September 21, 2026 8:44 AM To: comc <cpmc@collegeparkmd.gov> Subject: Al is a REAL Concern—We Need Guardrails (CivicPlus Renewal) Mayor and Council, Please consider pulling Item 26-G-92 (the CivicPlus renewal) off tonight's consent agenda so it can have a brief public discussion. To be clear up front, basic social media archiving is completely reasonable and necessary for public records compliance. Nobody has an issue with the city keeping good records. The concern comes from the Risk Management Analytics component in this subscription renewal. For those unfamiliar with the tech, | don't think RMA is just an electronic filing cabinet—it seems more like an automated surveillance tool: e Building resident profiles: It can track specific individuals across the city's socials over time, grading someone's "tone" or sentiment and essentially creating a digital dossier on how critical or supportive a resident is being. e Tracking momentum and quashing dissent: It uses automated keyword triggers to detect when an issue is gaining traction among residents, sending instant alerts to staff so public pushback can be managed or countered before it spreads. e Instant, unerasable logging: It scrapes and archives comments the second they are posted, capturing an immediate copy even if a resident misspoke, corrected themselves, or chose to delete the comment a moment later. Even if staff's intent is purely to archive records and nobody intends to touch those features, letting this pass on consent leaves too many loose ends: e Procuring only what we need: CivicPlus offers standard record retention. If we have no intention of profiling residents or monitoring public sentiment, we should adjust the contract to a basic archiving tier and avoid paying for tools we don't want. e Confirming technical settings first: Pausing to allow staff to verify with CivicPlus ahead of time whether those tracking features can be completely disabled or left off our account. There are real and legitimate concerns about this type of Al. e Setting clear guardrails: A simple, formal policy stating that the city uses archiving tools strictly for open-records compliance. Explicitly banning sentiment scoring and resident tracking would give the community peace of mind. Please take a few minutes to talk through it and make sure the contract fits what the city and its residents actually want. I'm happy to be corrected about the specifics on the record if I'm wrong—I think most would appreciate seeing due diligence by policymakers on this very controversial topic. text: APPROVED OCTOBER 5, 2026 MINUTES COMMISSIONERS OF POOLESVILLE September 21, 2026 *** This meeting was conducted live and streamed with live time posting to YouTube. Notice of the meeting date, time, and agenda were posted in advance, physically at the Town Hall, on the Town’s Website, and on social media. Before the start of the meeting, it was confirmed that the public could view the meeting on YouTube. Call to Order: President Brown called the meeting to order at 6:00 PM Commissioners Reed, Paksima, Bupp and Hobbs were in attendance. Town Manager Yost (virtual) was also in attendance. Adjourn to Closed Session: Commissioner Reed motioned to adjourn to a closed session pursuant to State Article 3-305(b)(i) to discuss the Town Manager applications/candidates. Second by Commissioner Paksima. Motion carries 5-0. Call to Order: President Brown called the meeting to order at 7:00 PM Commissioners Reed, Paksima, Bupp and Hobbs were in attendance. Town Manager Yost (virtual) and Assistant Manager Anderegg were also in attendance. Pledge of Allegiance: Commissioner Hobbs led the Pledge of Allegiance. Public Hearing: President Brown read the opening statement for Ordinance NO 236 – Use of Gold Carts on Municipal Roadways. Moment of Silence: President Brown offered condolences and requested a moment of silence in honor of Dakota Grimsby. Commissioner Reports/Announcements: Commissioner Hobbs discussed September 9th Parks Board meeting including Halmos Park parking, Fit to be Kids (Oct. 17th), ebikes, golf carts, and a street naming application. He also thanked everyone for their Poolesville Day efforts and announced the next Board meeting on October 7th and an upcoming rural roads discussion. Commissioner Bupp discussed the September 16th Planning meeting including Town Code definitions, street naming application and next meeting October 14th. Commissioner Paksima reported that Fair Access work on the Poolesville Day breakfast was a great success, new farm video, two muster emails coming up and the holiday event on December 13. Commissioner Reed discussed the updated advocacy sign, panel discussion, dinner for the arts and thanked Link Hoewing for his work. He also announced that Sustainable Poolesville would meet in October for mandatory training. President Brown discussed Poolesville Day, networking, commended Town Staff and Flag Committee and gave thanks to the Poolesville Day Committee. Public Comment None Approval of Minutes Commissioner Reed motioned to approve the August 17, 2026, minutes. Second, by Commissioner Paksima. Motion carried 4-0-1, with Commissioner Bupp abstaining. New Business Ordinance 237 – Sign Code Amendments - Introductions – Assistant Manager Anderegg provided the introduction. After a short discussion, Commissioner Paksima motioned to set a Public Hearing for October 5, 2026. Second by Commissioner Hobbs. Motion carried 5-0. Old Business: Ordinance NO. 235 – Accessory Dwelling Units: Assistant Manager Anderegg provided a summary of the ordinance and process. The Commissioners engaged in a discussion and determined that they would discuss it further at the next meeting. Town Manager Report Manager Yost and Assistant Manager Anderegg reported on: 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. Staff is winding down the design phase for the streetscape and preparing for the construction/bid Phase. Contractors have completed the walkway from Ferry Crossing to the John Poole House. The Town of Poolesville has entered into a 3-year agreement with the State to use salt during a snow emergency. This is our backup source, as we use the county first. The Town has been doing these agreements for the last decade or so. By charter, the Commissioners must approve these agreements; therefore, staff asks for the Commissioners' consent to execute the agreement. Thanks to Tara, Preston, and the rest of the Parks and Streets Department for all their hard work before and on Poolesville Day. The Steven’s Park pickleball courts were vandalized. The repair costs are estimated at $16,000. The Town will be filing an insurance claim for the damage. Adjournment Commissioner Bupp motioned to adjourn. Second by Commissioner Reed. Motion carried 5-0. Board of County Commissioners of Washington County, Maryland Agenda Report Form SUBJECT: Reclassification of a Master Deputy Position to a Sergeant Position PRESENTATION DATE: September 22, 2026 PRESENTATION BY: Major Joel Footen, Washington County Sheriff’s Office RECOMMENDED MOTION: Motion to approve the reclassification of one Master Deputy position to a Sergeant position within the Washington County Sheriff’s Office. REPORT-IN-BRIEF: During the FY2027 budget process, the Washington County Sheriff’s Office reclassified a Sergeant position to a Lieutenant position as part of an adjustment to the agency’s organizational structure and chain of command. At the time of that reclassification, the corresponding need to reclassify a Master Deputy position to a Sergeant position was inadvertently overlooked. This request corrects that oversight and ensures that the appropriate supervisory structure and span of control are maintained. DISCUSSION: The reclassification of one Master Deputy position to a Sergeant position is necessary to maintain the Sheriff’s Office chain of command and an appropriate span of control for supervisors. The previously approved reclassification of a Sergeant position to a Lieutenant position created a supervisory vacancy at the Sergeant level. Reclassifying an existing Master Deputy position to Sergeant will restore that supervisory level and provide appropriate oversight of personnel and day-to-day operations. This request does not add an additional position to the Sheriff’s Office authorized staffing complement. Rather, it reclassifies an existing position to maintain the organizational structure and supervisory coverage intended as part of the FY2027 budget process. FISCAL IMPACT: The position proposed for reclassification is Position #231. Current Master Deputy Salary (Grade 5, Step 8): $88,150 Sergeant Salary (Grade 7): $94,761 Annual Salary Difference: $6,611 The annual fiscal impact associated with the reclassification is approximately $6,611 in salary, excluding any associated changes in benefits. CONCURRENCES: County Administrator Michelle Gordon ALTERNATIVES: Deny the requested reclassification and maintain Position #231 at the Master Deputy classification. POLICY STATEMENT The Parks and Recreation Department is committed to providing a safe environment for all participants in athletic and recreational programs. This Concussion Management Policy established procedures for the recognition, removal, evaluation, and return-to-play of participants suspected of sustaining a concussion or other head injury. II. PURPOSE The purpose of this policy is to safeguard the health and safety of participants involved in athletic events and activities sponsored, organized, or authorized by the Parks & Recreation Department. Prompt recognition and proper management of concussions are essential to minimizing the risk of further injury and ensuring participant well-being. III. DEFINITION A concussion is a traumatic brain injury caused by a bump, blow, or jolt to the head or body that results in the rapid movement of the brain within the skull. IV. RECOGNITION OF SYMPTOMS Common signs and symptoms of concussions may include, but are not limited to: • Headache • Dizziness or balance problems • Nausea or vomiting • Confusion or memory problems • Blurred vision • Sensitivity to light or noise • Fatigue • Loss of consciousness Staff, coaches, volunteers, and officials shall report suspected concussions immediately to the Recreation Attendant on duty and an incident report shall be completed. Parents and participants are strongly encouraged to report suspected concussions immediately Recreation Attendant shall provide the notification and the incident report to on-site Program Director or Coordinator. V. REMOVAL FROM PARTICIPATION Any participant suspected of sustaining a concussion during a Parks and Recreation activity shall be: 1. Immediately removed from participation by the on-site Program Director or Coordinator. 2. “When in doubt, sit them out.” 3. Prohibited from returning to play or activity on the same day. 4. Observed for signs of worsening conditions. 5. Referred to a licensed healthcare provider for evaluation. The on-site Program Director or Coordinator shall provide a copy of the Incident Report and notification of concussion and removal to the Parks and Recreation Director as soon as practical. VI. EMERGENCY RESPONSE Emergency medical services (911) shall be contacted immediately if the participant exhibits any of the following: • Loss of consciousness • Repeated vomiting • Seizure activity • Difficulty breathing • Slurred speech • Unequal pupils • Significant confusion or deterioration • Neck injury concerns • Any other life-threatening condition Parents/guardians shall be notified as soon as practical. VII. MEDICAL EVALUATION AND CLEARANCE A participant diagnosed with a concussion shall not return to participation until: • Symptoms have resolved, and • Written medical clearance is provided by a licensed healthcare provider authorized to evaluate and manage concussions. Documentation of medical clearance must be submitted to the Parks and Recreation Director prior to resuming participation. VIII. RETURN-TO-PLAY PROCEDURE Participants returning after a concussion should follow a gradual, medically supervised progression of activity. If symptoms reappear during any stage of activity, participation shall stop immediately and medical reassessment shall occur. IX. DOCUMENTATION AND REPORTING Staff shall complete an incident report for all suspected concussions. Reports shall include: • Date/time of injury • Description of incident • Observed symptoms • Actions taken • Parent notification • Medical response information Records shall be maintained in accordance with applicable Maryland records retention requirements. X. EDUCATION AND TRAINING Coaches, staff, volunteers, and program participants are encouraged to complete concussion awareness education annually. Educational materials may be obtained from: XI. • CDC HEADS UP Concussion Program • National Recreation and Park Association COMPLIANCE Failure to comply with this policy may result in removal from participation, disciplinary action, or suspension from Parks and Recreation activities.
